question: A 24-year-old woman is found to have CIN 1 on colposcopy-directed biopsy after an abnormal Pap smear. She has no other risk factors and satisfactory colposcopy. Which statement best describes the expected natural history of her lesion?

answers.text: Approximately 60% of CIN 1 lesions will spontaneously regress over 2 years

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. About 60% of CIN 1 regresses spontaneously, ~30% persists, and only ~10% progresses to CIN 2/3. This underpins the conservative, surveillance-based approach to CIN 1.

answers.text: CIN 1 progresses to invasive cancer in approximately 30% of cases if untreated

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. CIN 1 progresses to invasive cancer in <1–2% of cases. It is CIN 3 that carries the highest progression risk (~30% over 30 years if untreated).

answers.text: CIN 1 should always be treated immediately to prevent progression

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Because >60% of CIN 1 regresses spontaneously, the standard management is surveillance rather than immediate ablation or excision.

answers.text: Regression of CIN 1 occurs only if the underlying HPV infection clears first, which is rare

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Clearance of HPV infection is actually common in young women, occurring in 60–80% within 1–2 years. Viral clearance is the biological mechanism driving CIN 1 regression.

overallFeedback.feedback: CIN 1 spontaneous regression rate is approximately 60%. Treatment is reserved for CIN 2/3 or persistent CIN 1 after 2 years of surveillance.
Correct. ~60% of CIN 1 regresses spontaneously — this is why surveillance, not immediate treatment, is standard.
